extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and instructors in probability theory and ergodic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conditions for defining stationary/ergodic processes and for applying Birkhoff's ergodic theorem, recurrence results, Kac's formula, and the subadditive ergodic theorem; includes examples and moment/tail conditions needed in applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: X0, X1, ... is said to be a stationary sequence if for every k, the shifted sequence {X_{k+n}, n ≥ 0} has the same distribution; equivalently for each m, (X0,...,Xm) and (Xk,...,Xk+m) have the same distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: (i) i.i.d. sequences; (ii) Markov chain started in a stationary distribution π (π(A) = ∫ π(dx) p(x,A)); (iii) rotation of the circle Xn(ω) = (ω + nθ) mod 1; (iv) sequences obtained from a measure-preserving map ϕ via Xn(ω) = X(ϕ^n ω). Kolmogorov's extension theorem shows that any 'nice' stationary sequence can be realized via the shift on sequence space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure-preserving transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A measurable map ϕ : Ω → Ω is measure preserving if P(ϕ^{-1}A) = P(A) for all A ∈ F. Given such a ϕ and a measurable X, Xn(ω) = X(ϕ^n ω) defines a stationary sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction (example 6.1.4) is the canonical setting used throughout the chapter; many examples (including rotations and the shift on sequence space) are special cases. It is the basic set-up for applying the ergodic theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant events and σ-field I
rubrics_metrics.description: A set A ∈ F is invariant if ϕ^{-1}A = A (equality modulo null sets). The collection I of invariant events is a σ-field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: I is used in statements of ergodic theorems: E(X|I) appears as the limiting time-average. Exercises ask to check I is a σ-field and properties of almost-invariant vs strictly invariant sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ergodicity (triviality of I)
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure-preserving transformation ϕ is ergodic if the invariant σ-field I is trivial, i.e., for every A ∈ I, P(A) ∈ {0,1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: no nontrivial invariant subsets of positive measure. Examples: (i) i.i.d. sequences are ergodic by Kolmogorov's 0-1 law (I ⊂ tail σ-field); (ii) a stationary Markov chain with countable state space and stationary distribution π with π(x)>0 for all x is ergodic iff the chain is irreducible and recurrent (periodicity causes T and I to differ); (iii) rotation of circle: ergodic iff θ is irrational (rational θ yields nontrivial invariant sets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Birkhoff's ergodic theorem — applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ is measure-preserving and X ∈ L1, then the time averages (1/n) ∑_{m=0}^{n-1} X(ϕ^m ω) converge a.s. and in L1 to E(X|I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the transformation is ergodic (I trivial), the limit equals EX, yielding classical results such as the strong law of large numbers for i.i.d. sequences. The theorem is called 'pointwise' or 'individual' ergodic theorem because of almost-sure convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yosida–Kakutani maximal ergodic lemma (tool/criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X_j(ω)=X(ϕ^j ω), S_k = ∑_{i=0}^{k-1} X_i, M_k = max(0, S_1, ..., S_k). Then E(X; M_k > 0) ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inequality is a key ingredient in the standard proof of the ergodic theorem. The text gives the inequality and its proof and uses it to deduce limsup Sn/n ≤ 0 under suitable centering.

rubrics_metrics.name: L1 → Lp strengthening (exercise criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X ∈ L^p with p > 1 then the convergence in Birkhoff's ergodic theorem occurs in L^p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises indicate further variants: (i) dominated conditions on sequences g_n give almost-sure/time-average convergence to E(g|I); (ii) if g_n → g in L1 then the convergence is in L1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence criterion for stationary integer-valued walks
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.3.2: Let X_i be stationary integer-valued with E|X_i|<∞, S_n = ∑_{i=1}^n X_i, and A = {S_k ≠ 0 ∀ k ≥1}. (i) If E(X1|I)=0 then P(A)=0 (i.e., recurrence). (ii) If P(A)=0 then P(S_n=0 i.o.)=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: conditional mean zero (w.r.t. invariant σ-field) implies recurrence—averaging via ergodic theorem gives Sn/n → 0. The conditional mean is needed to rule out mixtures of positive/negative drifts (e.g., half the time all +1, half all −1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Range asymptotics via ergodic theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.3.1: For a stationary sequence X_i in R^d with S_k = ∑_{i=1}^k X_i, let A = {S_k ≠ 0 ∀ k ≥1} and R_n = |{S_1,...,S_n}|. Then R_n/n → E(1_A | I) almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses lower and upper bounds expressed as time averages and applies Birkhoff to obtain the limit as a conditional expectation. In the ergodic case, the limit is P(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kac's return-time formula and stationarity of interarrival times
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.3.3: If P(event A occurs at least once)=1, then under P(·|X0 ∈ A) the interarrival times t_n = T_n − T_{n-1} form a stationary sequence and E(T1 | X0 ∈ A) = 1 / P(X0 ∈ A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generalizes Markov-chain mean return-time results. Proof constructs a two-sided stationary sequence and uses disjointness of certain backward events; gives formula Ex T_x = 1/π(x) when specialized to Markov chains with stationary distribution π.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subadditive ergodic theorem — applicability conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 6.4.1: For random variables X_{m,n}, 0 ≤ m < n, require (i) X_{0,m} + X_{m,n} ≥ X_{0,n} (subadditivity); (ii) for each k, the sequence {X_{nk,(n+1)k}, n ≥1} is stationary; (iii) distribution of {X_{m,m+k}, k ≥1} does not depend on m; (iv) E(X^+_{0,1}) < ∞ and for each n, E X_{0,n} ≥ γ_0 n for some γ_0 > −∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under these hypotheses: (a) lim_{n→∞} E X_{0,n}/n = inf_m E X_{0,m}/m ≡ γ; (b) X = lim_{n→∞} X_{0,n}/n exists a.s. and in L1 with EX = γ; (c) if the stationary sequences in (ii) are ergodic then X = γ a.s. The text discusses Kingman's original formulation and Liggett's variant used here and provides a detailed proof with four steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moment / tail conditions in applications of subadditive theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete sufficient integrability conditions used in applications: e.g., for products of random positive matrices assume E|log A_m(i,j)| < ∞ for all i,j; for first-passage percolation assume the tail condition ∫_0^∞ (1 − F(x))^{2d} dx < ∞ (equivalently the minimum of 2d i.i.d. edge times has finite mean) to ensure finite limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These application-specific moment/tail conditions are the practical criteria to check before applying the subadditive ergodic theorem; the chapter gives worked examples showing how these conditions enter and why they are (in some cases) necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation-of-circle ergodicity criterion (equidistribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the dynamical system ϕ(x) = (x + θ) mod 1 on [0,1) with Lebesgue measure: if θ = m/n rational then ϕ is not ergodic; if θ is irrational then ϕ is ergodic (in fact any invariant L2 function must be constant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Fourier expansion in L2: f(ϕ(x)) = f(x) forces vanishing of Fourier coefficients for k ≠ 0 when e^{2π i k θ} ≠ 1, i.e., θ irrational. Consequence: Weyl equidistribution and applications like Benford's law for sequences 2^m via fractional parts of m log_10 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ergodic theorem to recover classical laws (SLLN, equidistribution, Benford)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specializations of Birkhoff's theorem yield classical results: for i.i.d. sequences it gives the strong law of large numbers; for irrational rotations it yields Weyl's equidistribution theorem and hence Benford's law for sequences like 2^m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights these as canonical checks: verifying the Birkhoff hypotheses on familiar examples recovers well-known limit laws, illustrating how to apply the theorem in practice.
